chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
title: The band as a family; Bobby Stark
summary: McRae explains rehearsals as corrections among equals, including trumpeter Bobby Stark, whose solos other bands imitated.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: This band was like a family. If you would do something wrong, I'd tell you. I'd say, "Look, that's wrong. You ain't playing that right," you know. "Do this, do that."
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

That's what made those bands in those days great, because everybody worked together. They didn't have, like, hire a man, you're just here, just playing your horn. You was like, become a part of the band. And you'd have to be that type to live with this, because you couldn't be an outsider. Everybody would be together. And so, that's why we got -- a lot of things we'd call rehearsal. And these rehearsals was to iron out the mistakes going on in the band. We didn't care whose feelings it hurt, because if we hurt your feelings, you didn't belong in there. You got to be able to take directions, to stand this. (Inaudible), "Look, so and so and so." We had like Bobby Stark. We know he drank a lot and Bobby would listen to us. He would stop. He would cool down and, "Okay," but he was one great trumpet player. Bobby Stark -- all the great white trumpet players admired Bobby Stark. He

was such a great trumpet player in his days -- those times.
The ones in (Inaudible) Casa Loma, "Hey, man," -- they'd steal his solos -- all those guys. Even Benny Goodman's men. They used to like the way --
You hear some of the things that Benny Goodman play, you hear some of the things --
If you listen to some of the trumpet players and you play some of Chick Webb's records on Bobby Stark, a lot of guys are playing like Bobby Stark's style back in those days.
